﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ ﴿and you see people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾ ﴿then glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness﴾ [Al-Nasr: 3].

(*Idhā*) is an indefinite temporal noun whose extent is determined by the content of the clause that follows it. *Idhā* is thus a general temporal noun, and it is most often used for the future. For this reason it is often given the meaning of a conditional, and the verb that follows it is usually in the past form, to indicate that the event is certain. It may also be followed by a present-tense verb, as in God's words: ﴿And He is capable of gathering them whenever He wills﴾ [Al-Shura: 29].

It is also used for the past. In that case the clause after it must be in the past form, and *idhā* does not then carry the meaning of a condition. It is merely informative, without intending a conditional connection, as in God's words: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush toward it﴾ [Al-Jumu'ah: 11].

Here *idhā* carries the meaning of a condition without doubt, because of the particle *fa* (then) in His words: ﴿so glorify your Lord﴾ [Al-Nasr: 3]. The question of whether it refers to the future or not has already been discussed.

*Al-nasr* (help) means aid against an enemy. The help of God is followed by prevailing over the enemy. *Al-fatḥ* (victory/conquest) means taking possession of the land and territory of the enemy, since it happens through opening the gate of a city, as in God's words: ﴿Enter upon them through the gate, and when you have entered it, you will surely be victorious﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 23]. It also happens by breaking into the frontier points and strongholds of the land, for they used to descend upon lands that had ravines and passes. Labid said:

*And the darkness of night concealed the vulnerable points of the frontiers.*

The Muslims had already conquered Khaybar before the revelation of this verse, so it is established that the conquest mentioned in it is another conquest, namely the conquest of Makkah. This is indicated by the definite article of prior reference (*al-'ahd*), and it is the well-known conquest referred to in God's words: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [Al-Fath: 1] ﴿that God may forgive you your earlier and later sins, complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path﴾ [Al-Fath: 2] ﴿and that God may help you with mighty help﴾ [Al-Fath: 3].

The attribution of *nasr* (help) to *Allah* indicates the magnification of this help, and that it is a mighty help that breaks the normal course, for God took care to bring about its causes, and it did not follow the customary pattern in which events arise from similar causes. *Jā'a* (came) is used here, figuratively, in the sense of "occurred and was realised."

[Page 591]

The definite article in *al-fatḥ* (the victory) is of prior reference, and God had promised His Messenger (ﷺ) this more than once. Among these is God's words: ﴿Indeed, He who imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to a place of return﴾ [Al-Qasas: 85], and His words: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, God willing, secure, with your heads shaved and your hair cut short, not fearing anyone. He knew what you did not know, and He granted you besides that a near victory﴾ [Al-Fath: 27]. This verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and that was before the revelation of the Surah "When the help of God comes," according to all opinions.

The exegetes from the earliest generations onward have agreed that the conquest mentioned in this surah is the conquest of Makkah, except for a report from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that it was the conquest of cities and palaces, meaning the fortresses. The conquest of Makkah preoccupied the minds of all the Arabs. The Muslims hoped for it and knew what the Qur'an had alluded to of the promise. The people of Makkah anticipated it, and the rest of the Arabs awaited what the outcome would be between the people of Makkah and the Prophet (ﷺ). They held back from entering Islam until the conquest of Makkah, saying: "If Muhammad prevails over his people, then he is a prophet." It often happened that some would prevent others who wished to follow Islam from entering it, and would have them wait to see whether the power of Islam or the power of polytheism would prevail.

Al-Bukhari reported from 'Amr ibn Salamah, who said: "When the conquest came, every people hastened to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with their Islam, and the tribes were holding back from embracing Islam until the conquest of Makkah. They would say: 'Leave him and his people; if he prevails over them, then he is a prophet.'"

And from al-Hasan: "When Makkah was conquered, the Arabs turned to one another and said: 'Since he has triumphed over the people of the Sacred Precinct, we have no power against him.' So they entered Islam in multitudes."

According to the majority view that the conquest is the conquest of Makkah, it is correct that this surah was revealed after the conquest of Khaybar, and this is the view of most scholars regarding the time of its revelation.

It is possible, according to those who say it was revealed after the battle of Hunayn, that the conquest had already occurred, and the conditional is then connected to the whole of the conquest of Makkah, the coming of another help from God, and the entry of people into Islam. This refers to what was granted to him afterwards, and the entry of all the Arabs into Islam in the Year of Delegations (*sanat al-wufūd*).

According to what is reported from Ibn 'Umar, that it was revealed at the Farewell Pilgrimage (*Ḥijjat al-Wadā'*), the conditional clause in His words, ﴿so glorify your Lord﴾ [Al-Nasr: 3], is connected to a past condition, intended as a reminder that it has already taken place. That is: when what We promised you of help, conquest, and the spread of Islam throughout the lands of the Arabs has come to pass, then glorify your Lord with His praise. This is what those exegetes meant who said that *idhā* here has the sense of *qad* (indeed). This is an explanation of the meaning, and *idhā* is not one of the particles that come with the meaning of *qad*.

The seeing in His words, ﴿and you see the people﴾, may be a knowing (*'ilmiyyah*), meaning: you know with certainty that people enter the religion of God in multitudes. This knowledge comes through reports arriving from the horizons of the Arab lands and the dwelling places of their tribes, and from those who come to him from their delegations. In this case, the clause ﴿entering﴾ is in the place of the second object of *ra'ayta* (you saw/knew).

It may also be a visual seeing (*baṣariyyah*), in that he saw the multitudes of Arab delegations coming to Madinah and entering Islam, and that was in the ninth year. The Prophet (ﷺ) saw with his own eyes what showed him that they would all enter Islam, through those who were present with him at the standing place during the Farewell Pilgrimage. They numbered a hundred thousand from the various tribes of the Arabs. In this case, the clause ﴿entering﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) relating to *al-nās* (the people).

The religion of God is Islam, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19], and His words: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition of God upon which He created mankind﴾ [Al-Rum: 30].

Entering into the religion is a metaphor for uttering the testimony of faith and committing oneself to the rulings of the religion that result from that testimony. The religion is likened to a house or an enclosure, in the mode of the implicit metaphor (*makniyyah*), and it is indicated by something that belongs to the likened thing, namely entering. This is based on likening the attachment to the religion to the state of something contained being within a container. Therefore there is also an explicit metaphor (*taṣrīḥiyyah*) within it.

*Al-nās* (the people) is a collective noun denoting a group of human beings. This was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 8], in Surah al-Baqarah. When the word *nās* is made definite with the article, it may indicate a specific prior reference, as in His words: ﴿those to whom the people said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], or it may indicate the category as a whole, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], or it may indicate comprehensiveness, as in His words: ﴿And among the people is he who says﴾ and His words: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ [Al-Nas: 1].

The definite article in this verse is for customary comprehensiveness (*al-istighrāq al-'urfī*), meaning all the people who come to mind, since it is not intended to refer to specific known individuals, and because it is impossible for every individual to enter the religion of God, as the observed reality shows. Thus the meaning is: you saw many people, or you saw the Arabs.

[Page 593]

Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr al-Namari, may God have mercy on him, said in his book *al-Isti'ab*, in the section on Khirash al-Hudhali: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not die while there remained a single unbelieving man among the Arabs. Rather, all of them had entered Islam after Hunayn and al-Ta'if; some came in person, and some sent their representatives." [End of quotation.]

What is meant is the Arabs of the Hijaz, Najd, and Yemen, because among the Arabs of Syria and Iraq there were those who had not entered Islam. These were Taghlib and Ghassan on the borders of Syria, and likewise Lakhm and Kalb from Iraq. These were Christians, and those among them who embraced Islam did so only after the conquest of Syria and Iraq following the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Therefore the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not see them entering the religion of God with his own eyes.

It is possible that God informed him of this, if we take the seeing to be a knowing.

*Al-afwāj* is the plural of *fawj*, which means a large group. This was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿This is a host rushing in with you﴾ [Sad: 59], in Surah Sad. Here it means that they enter Islam. *Afwājan* (in multitudes) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) referring to the pronoun in *yadkhulūn* (they enter).

The clause ﴿so glorify your Lord with His praise﴾ [Al-Nasr: 3] is the response (*jawāb*) of *idhā*, in view of the conditional meaning it contains. The verb *fa-sabbiḥ* (so glorify) is what governs *idhā* in the accusative as an adverb of time. The *fa* (then) links the response, because it is a verb of performative command (*fi'l inshā'*).

He combined glorification with praise using the *bā'* of accompaniment (*bā' al-muṣāḥabah*), which requires that the glorification follows the praise, since the *bā'* of accompaniment has the meaning of *ma'a* (with). Like *ma'a*, it is attached to the thing accompanied. Thus praising God for the attainment of the help, the conquest, and the entry of the people into Islam was something already accomplished, and did not require a command to perform it, because it was the custom of the Messenger (ﷺ) to have already done it. Rather, he needed to be reminded of a particular glorification that had not occurred before in his glorifications, and a particular seeking of forgiveness that had not occurred before in his seeking of forgiveness.

It is possible that the glorification commanded is a glorification of joy and wonder at God's facilitation for him of what no one would imagine could be accomplished for him. Indeed, "Glory be to God" and similar expressions are used to express wonder, as in the words of al-A'sha:

*When his boasting reached me, I said: Glory be to Alqamah the boaster!*

In placing the command to glorify and praise before the command to seek forgiveness, there is a preparation for the granting of his request for forgiveness, following the custom of the Arabs of placing praise before asking for a need, as Ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*If a man praises you one day, praise itself spares him from having to ask.*

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) never ceased glorifying God, so what is intended is a glorification that accompanies the praise for what he was given of help, conquest, and the entry of the community into Islam.

The conjoining of the command to seek God's forgiveness with the command to glorify with praise indicates that it belongs to the scope of the response to *idhā*, and that it is a seeking of forgiveness that takes place together with praise, like what was established in ﴿so glorify your Lord with His praise﴾ [Al-Nasr: 3]. This indicates that it is a particular seeking of forgiveness, because the general seeking of forgiveness, which covers asking for pardon for shortcomings and the like, had already been commanded earlier, and it is among the Prophet's (ﷺ) customary acts. He said: "Indeed, there comes over my heart a veil, so I seek God's forgiveness a hundred times a day and night."

Therefore, linking the command to glorify and seek forgiveness to the attainment of help and conquest is an allusion to a glorification and forgiveness through which a closeness to God is achieved that had not been intended before. This closeness is preparation for meeting God, and an indication that his worldly life was nearing its end, and that the acts of worship and devotions which raise the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) with his Lord were coming to completion. Nothing remained except that he should ask his Lord to overlook what befalls him of preoccupation with some of the necessities of life, or of preoccupation with an important matter concerning the community, through which something else more important might be missed. Such was the ransoming of the captives of Badr, when the goal of their annihilation, which would have been better for the community, was lost. For this, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was rebuked by God's words: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives﴾ [Al-Anfal: 67], and the verse continues. Or it may be due to human necessities such as sleep and food, which reduce the state of resemblance to the angels, who glorify God night and day without ceasing. This was thus a notice of the approach of the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), through his passing from a life that bears the burdens of the message to an everlasting life among the heavenly, angelic realms.

The discourse is of the nature of allusive metonymy (*kināyah ramziyyah*), and this does not exclude the intention of the explicit meaning, namely that the command to glorify and seek forgiveness is understood as a command to increase the saying of these words. The discernment of the speech has indicated this meaning to some of the Companions who had penetrating understanding, and they delved into it, such as Abu Bakr, 'Umar, al-'Abbas, his son 'Abd Allah, and Ibn Mas'ud. Regarding Muqatil: "When it was revealed, he recited it..."

The Prophet ﷺ came to his Companions, and they rejoiced and were glad. Al-'Abbas wept, so the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "What makes you weep, uncle?" He said: "Your soul has been announced to you." Then he said: "It is indeed as you say." ) In another narration: "It was revealed at Mina, and 'Umar and al-'Abbas wept. They were asked about this, and they said: 'In it the Messenger of Allah has been informed of his death.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'You have spoken truthfully; my soul has been announced to me.'"

In Sahih al-Bukhari and elsewhere, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: 'Umar used to admit the people of Badr (Ahl Badr, the Companions who fought at the Battle of Badr) and admitted me along with them. Some of them felt resentment about this, so 'Umar said to them: "He is one of whom you know." He said: So one day he admitted them, and admitted me along with them. He asked them about this surah, "When the help of Allah comes, and the conquest" (﴿إذا جاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ والفَتْحُ﴾). They said: "Allah commanded His Prophet that when victory was granted to him, he should seek His forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance." Then he said: "What do you say, Ibn 'Abbas?" I said: "It is not so, but Allah informed His Prophet of the approach of his term, saying: ﴿When the help of Allah comes, and the conquest﴾; that is the sign of your death." 'Umar said: "I know of it nothing except what you say." This is the understanding of 'Umar, al-'Abbas, and his son 'Abd Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: It is narrated that when it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivered a sermon and said: "Indeed, a servant was given the choice by Allah between this world and what is with Allah, and he chose what is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." Abu Bakr understood, and said: "We ransom you with our souls, our wealth, our fathers, and our children." (End of quotation.)

Ibn Hajar said in his takhrij (documentation) of the hadiths of al-Kashshaf: "The hadith is agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim) except its beginning, that it was at the time of the revelation of the surah." (End of quotation.) It is possible that Abu Bakr's weeping occurred twice: the first time at the revelation of Surat al-Nasr, as in the narration of al-Kashshaf, and the second time at the Prophet's ﷺ sermon during his illness.

It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that this surah is called Surat al-Tawdi' (the Surah of Farewell), meaning that they knew it was an announcement of the approaching death of the Messenger ﷺ.

The placement of glorifying (tasbih) and praising (hamd) before seeking forgiveness (istighfar) is because tasbih refers to describing Allah, Exalted is He, as transcendent above deficiency, and it encompasses attributes of negation; so tasbih is purely directed toward the side of Allah, Exalted is He. And because hamd is praise of Allah for His bounty, and it is the servant's fulfilment of what is incumbent upon him in thanking the Benefactor, it necessarily entails affirming the attributes of perfection for Allah, which are the source of His bounty to His servant. Thus it combines the side of Allah and the share of the servant. As for istighfar, it is a share for the servant alone, since it is his request that Allah pardon what He would hold him accountable for.

[Page 596]

The apparent expectation would be that it say: "So glorify Him with His praise" (فَسَبِّحَ بِحَمْدِهِ), since the Name of Majesty (Allah) was mentioned earlier in His words: "When the help of Allah comes" (﴿إذا جاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ﴾). Instead, it turned from the pronoun to the explicit noun, "your Lord" (رَبُّكَ). This is because the attribute "Lord" (Rabb) and its being annexed to the pronoun of address carry an allusion that among the wisdom of that help and conquest, and the entry of people into Islam, is a blessing that Allah bestowed upon him when this great good came about through him. This is an honour to him, a care for him, and it is the manner of the Lord's gentleness toward the one He nurtures; for its meaning is sovereignty joined with gentleness and bringing to perfection.

The speech has ended at His words "and seek His forgiveness" (واسْتَغْفِرْهُ). It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ, in his recitation, would pause at "and seek His forgiveness" (واسْتَغْفِرْهُ), then complete the surah.

He combined glorification with praise using the *bā'* of accompaniment (*bā' al-muṣāḥabah*), which requires that the glorification follows the praise, since the *bā'* of accompaniment has the meaning of *ma'a* (with). Like *ma'a*, it is attached to the thing accompanied. Thus praising God for the attainment of the help, the conquest, and the entry of the people into Islam was something already accomplished, and did not require a command to perform it, because it was the custom of the Messenger (ﷺ) to have already done it. Rather, he needed to be reminded of a particular glorification that had not occurred before in his glorifications, and a particular seeking of forgiveness that had not occurred before in his seeking of forgiveness.

It is possible that the glorification commanded is a glorification of joy and wonder at God's facilitation for him of what no one would imagine could be accomplished for him. Indeed, "Glory be to God" and similar expressions are used to express wonder, as in the words of al-A'sha:

*When his boasting reached me, I said: Glory be to Alqamah the boaster!*

In placing the command to glorify and praise before the command to seek forgiveness, there is a preparation for the granting of his request for forgiveness, following the custom of the Arabs of placing praise before asking for a need, as Ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*If a man praises you one day, praise itself spares him from having to ask.*

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) never ceased glorifying God, so what is intended is a glorification that accompanies the praise for what he was given of help, conquest, and the entry of the community into Islam.

The conjoining of the command to seek God's forgiveness with the command to glorify with praise indicates that it belongs to the scope of the response to *idhā*, and that it is a seeking of forgiveness that takes place together with praise, like what was established in ﴿so glorify your Lord with His praise﴾ [Al-Nasr: 3]. This indicates that it is a particular seeking of forgiveness, because the general seeking of forgiveness, which covers asking for pardon for shortcomings and the like, had already been commanded earlier, and it is among the Prophet's (ﷺ) customary acts. He said: "Indeed, there comes over my heart a veil, so I seek God's forgiveness a hundred times a day and night."

Therefore, linking the command to glorify and seek forgiveness to the attainment of help and conquest is an allusion to a glorification and forgiveness through which a closeness to God is achieved that had not been intended before. This closeness is preparation for meeting God, and an indication that his worldly life was nearing its end, and that the acts of worship and devotions which raise the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) with his Lord were coming to completion. Nothing remained except that he should ask his Lord to overlook what befalls him of preoccupation with some of the necessities of life, or of preoccupation with an important matter concerning the community, through which something else more important might be missed. Such was the ransoming of the captives of Badr, when the goal of their annihilation, which would have been better for the community, was lost. For this, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was rebuked by God's words: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives﴾ [Al-Anfal: 67], and the verse continues. Or it may be due to human necessities such as sleep and food, which reduce the state of resemblance to the angels, who glorify God night and day without ceasing. This was thus a notice of the approach of the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), through his passing from a life that bears the burdens of the message to an everlasting life among the heavenly, angelic realms.

The discourse is of the nature of allusive metonymy (*kināyah ramziyyah*), and this does not exclude the intention of the explicit meaning, namely that the command to glorify and seek forgiveness is understood as a command to increase the saying of these words. The discernment of the speech has indicated this meaning to some of the Companions who had penetrating understanding, and they delved into it, such as Abu Bakr, 'Umar, al-'Abbas, his son 'Abd Allah, and Ibn Mas'ud. Regarding Muqatil: "When it was revealed, he recited it..."

The Prophet ﷺ came to his Companions, and they rejoiced and were glad. Al-'Abbas wept, so the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "What makes you weep, uncle?" He said: "Your soul has been announced to you." Then he said: "It is indeed as you say." ) In another narration: "It was revealed at Mina, and 'Umar and al-'Abbas wept. They were asked about this, and they said: 'In it the Messenger of Allah has been informed of his death.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'You have spoken truthfully; my soul has been announced to me.'"

In Sahih al-Bukhari and elsewhere, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: 'Umar used to admit the people of Badr (Ahl Badr, the Companions who fought at the Battle of Badr) and admitted me along with them. Some of them felt resentment about this, so 'Umar said to them: "He is one of whom you know." He said: So one day he admitted them, and admitted me along with them. He asked them about this surah, "When the help of Allah comes, and the conquest" (﴿إذا جاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ والفَتْحُ﴾). They said: "Allah commanded His Prophet that when victory was granted to him, he should seek His forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance." Then he said: "What do you say, Ibn 'Abbas?" I said: "It is not so, but Allah informed His Prophet of the approach of his term, saying: ﴿When the help of Allah comes, and the conquest﴾; that is the sign of your death." 'Umar said: "I know of it nothing except what you say." This is the understanding of 'Umar, al-'Abbas, and his son 'Abd Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: It is narrated that when it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivered a sermon and said: "Indeed, a servant was given the choice by Allah between this world and what is with Allah, and he chose what is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." Abu Bakr understood, and said: "We ransom you with our souls, our wealth, our fathers, and our children." (End of quotation.)

Ibn Hajar said in his takhrij (documentation) of the hadiths of al-Kashshaf: "The hadith is agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim) except its beginning, that it was at the time of the revelation of the surah." (End of quotation.) It is possible that Abu Bakr's weeping occurred twice: the first time at the revelation of Surat al-Nasr, as in the narration of al-Kashshaf, and the second time at the Prophet's ﷺ sermon during his illness.

It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that this surah is called Surat al-Tawdi' (the Surah of Farewell), meaning that they knew it was an announcement of the approaching death of the Messenger ﷺ.

The placement of glorifying (tasbih) and praising (hamd) before seeking forgiveness (istighfar) is because tasbih refers to describing Allah, Exalted is He, as transcendent above deficiency, and it encompasses attributes of negation; so tasbih is purely directed toward the side of Allah, Exalted is He. And because hamd is praise of Allah for His bounty, and it is the servant's fulfilment of what is incumbent upon him in thanking the Benefactor, it necessarily entails affirming the attributes of perfection for Allah, which are the source of His bounty to His servant. Thus it combines the side of Allah and the share of the servant. As for istighfar, it is a share for the servant alone, since it is his request that Allah pardon what He would hold him accountable for.

[Page 596]

The apparent expectation would be that it say: "So glorify Him with His praise" (فَسَبِّحَ بِحَمْدِهِ), since the Name of Majesty (Allah) was mentioned earlier in His words: "When the help of Allah comes" (﴿إذا جاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ﴾). Instead, it turned from the pronoun to the explicit noun, "your Lord" (رَبُّكَ). This is because the attribute "Lord" (Rabb) and its being annexed to the pronoun of address carry an allusion that among the wisdom of that help and conquest, and the entry of people into Islam, is a blessing that Allah bestowed upon him when this great good came about through him. This is an honour to him, a care for him, and it is the manner of the Lord's gentleness toward the one He nurtures; for its meaning is sovereignty joined with gentleness and bringing to perfection.

The speech has ended at His words "and seek His forgiveness" (واسْتَغْفِرْهُ). It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ, in his recitation, would pause at "and seek His forgiveness" (واسْتَغْفِرْهُ), then complete the surah.

**[Page 597]**

﴿Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.﴾

This is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) for the whole preceding discourse, and a causal explanation (*ta'lil*) for what in it calls for explanation, namely the command to seek forgiveness from his Lord, in view of the explicit meaning of the preceding discourse, as will become clear to you.

*Tawwab* is an intensive form (*mithal mubalagha*) from *taba 'alayhi*. The verb *taba*, when transitive with the particle *'ala*, is used in the sense of "granted the ability to repent." Lisan al-'Arab and al-Qamus affirm this usage, and it is specific to what is attributed to God.

The sentence contains four emphatics: *inna*, *kana*, the intensive form *tawwab*, and the *tanwin* of exaltation (*tanwin al-ta'zim*) on it.

Since the emphasis by *inna* here is not intended to refute denial or remove doubt, for neither of these can be supposed on the part of the one addressed (ﷺ), *inna* is purely for conveying concern with the information by stressing it. It has been established that when *inna* comes in this manner it serves the function of the particle of sequence and causation (*fa'* al-tartib wa al-tasabbub), conveying causation and linking the statement to what precedes it, as the *fa'* would. This has been discussed more than once, including at God's words ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Baqara: 32] in Surat al-Baqara. Thus the meaning is: He is exceedingly accepting of the repentance of His servants, and His acceptance of it is abundant.

Since the discourse is a concluding statement and causal explanation of the preceding discourse, it is necessary that the object of *tawwaban* be omitted and be understood as something like: "to those who repent." This understood object is intended in its generality, and this generality is restricted by the will of God, which the evidences of the attribute of Lordship (*rububiyya*) specify. When the evidence for the generality was mentioned right after the command to seek forgiveness, it conveyed that whenever he seeks forgiveness, He forgives him. This is an indication required by the implications of the structures. Thus this sentence conveys the causal explanation of the command to seek forgiveness, because seeking forgiveness is a request for pardon, and the one who requests awaits the granting of his request. As for the command in the sentence to glorify and praise (*tasbih* and *hamd*), it needs no causal explanation, because they are acts of declaring God free of imperfection and of praising Him.

Beyond this, the sentence also conveys an allusion to a promise of good acceptance with God, the Exalted, when one comes before the sacred realm (*al-'alam al-qudsi*). This is a metonymic meaning (*ma'na kinā'i*), because whoever is known for accepting the repentance of penitents is of a nature to honor the visit of those who visit him, who have striven with all their effort to please him to the utmost of their ability. Or it is a metaphor (*majaz*) through the relation of customary implication, because the utmost thing that loved ones fear at the time of meeting is the bitterness of reproach. So the report that He is *tawwab* implies that He does not fear reproach.

Thus this sentence, with its explicit meaning, its metonymic or metaphorical meaning, and its implications, is a causal explanation of what the sentence before it contained of an explicit or metonymic meaning appropriate to such explanation. The glorification and praise, considered as a preparation for the command to seek forgiveness, as stated just before, do not need explanation; or the causal explanation of what they prepare for suffices, so that it need not explain them. However, they, insofar as they are a symbol of the approach of the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), make what is in His words ﴿Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾ a promise of good acceptance, serving as causal explanation for their metonymic meaning. As for the command to seek forgiveness, the suitability of the causal explanation for it by His words ﴿Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾ holds with regard to both its explicit and metonymic meanings. That is: He accepts your seeking forgiveness and receives you with the best acceptance, as is the custom of one known for pardon and generosity.

The verb *kana* here is used in the implied sense of the continuous attribution of the quality in the past time, namely that this quality is intrinsic to Him, and its effect does not fail regarding His servants. Survey of the Qur'an indicates that God reports this about Himself from the beginning of creation. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqara: 37].

By the apparent standard, it should have been said: "Indeed, He is ever Forgiving," as in the verse ﴿So I said: Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed, He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nuh: 10]. Then the description would follow what suits His words "and seek His forgiveness." But this was set aside out of gentleness toward the Prophet (ﷺ), since his command to seek forgiveness does not necessarily imply that he has committed a sin, given what you have just learned, that the description *tawwaban* comes from *taba 'alayhi*, which is used in the sense of "granted him the ability to repent." This is an allusion that his command to seek forgiveness is a guidance to the station of good manners toward God, the Exalted, for He is not questioned about what He does with His servants, except that He graciously explained to them what He wills. Also, the description *tawwaban* is more suitable for forming the rhyme with the rhyme of *afwaja*, because the letter *jim* and the letter *ba'* are both among the letters described as stopped (*shidda*), unlike the letter *ra'*, which is among the letters whose quality is between stopped and fricative (*rakhawa*).

It is related in the Sahih, from A'isha, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not pray any prayer after the revelation of the sura ﴿When the victory of God comes, and the conquest﴾ [al-Nasr: 1] except that he would say: 'Glory be to You, our Lord, and praise be to You. O God, forgive me,' interpreting the Qur'an." That is, he interpreted the command in His words ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise, and seek His forgiveness﴾ according to its outward meaning, just as he interpreted it on another occasion as referring to the approach of his own death (ﷺ).

**[Page 599]**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Masad

This sura is named in most copies of the Qur'an "Surat Tabbat," and al-Tirmidhi likewise titled it in his Jami' and in most books of tafsir (exegesis), naming it after the first word in it.

It is named in some copies and in some tafsirs "Surat al-Masad." Al-Suyuti in al-Itqan limited himself to these two names.

A group of exegetes named it "Surat Abi Lahab," with the implied sense "the sura mentioning Abu Lahab." Abu Hayyan titled it in his tafsir "Surat al-Lahab," and I have not seen this from anyone else.

Ibn al-'Arabi titled it in Ahkam al-Qur'an "Surat ma kana min Abi Lahab," which is a title (*unwan*) and not a name.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the sixth sura in order of revelation; it was revealed after Surat al-Fatiha and before Surat al-Takwir.

Its number of verses is five.

It is related that its revelation was in the fourth year of the call (*al-ba'tha*). Its occasion of revelation, according to what is in the two Sahihs from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ascended one day upon al-Safa and called out, 'Ya sabahah!' (a word used to call for warning of an enemy who attacks people at morning). Quraysh gathered around him, and he said: 'I am a warner to you before a severe punishment. Tell me, if I informed you that an enemy would attack you in the evening or in the morning, would you believe me?' They said: 'We have never found you lying.' Abu Lahab said: 'May you perish all day! Did you gather us for this?' Then the revelation came: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾."

It occurs in the two Sahihs, from the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 214] and your people among them, the sincere ones, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out until he ascended al-Safa," up to the end of the previous hadith.

It is known that the verse ﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 214] is from Surat al-Shu'ara, which was revealed later than Surat Tabbat. The interpretation of this is that a verse resembling the verse of Surat al-Shu'ara was revealed before Surat Abi Lahab, because of what Abu Usama related, reaching Ibn 'Abbas: "When there was revealed ﴿And warn your nearest kindred and your people, the sincere ones among them﴾, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out until he ascended al-Safa." (He did not say "from Surat al-Shu'ara.") Thus it is established that the verse of Surat al-Shu'ara resembles the beginning of the verse that was revealed before the revelation of Surat Abi Lahab.

The rebuke of Abu Lahab for his saying "May you perish! Did you gather us for this?" and his threat for that; and the threat against his wife for supporting her husband and for her hatred of the Prophet (ﷺ).
